title: Why rebranding a charity is more dangerous than rebranding a company
dek: Mercy Corps changed its name to Prosper Global not because its strategy changed, but because the old name no longer fit what it was already doing — and in conflict zones, a name change can put staff more at risk.
why: Medium information density. The first half covers the disaster context and the rebranding logic; the second half, on the erosion of international humanitarian law and AI's entry into aid, is more valuable.
who: Founders and investors watching international aid, nonprofit branding and operations, and how geopolitics transmits into food and energy supply chains.
skip: From 16:53 to 18:59 is a sponsor ad and a promo for another podcast; you can skip it.

points.h: The name change isn't a strategy shift — the old name can't hold the new business
points.body: Jada says an organization's identity grows like a person's. The name Mercy Corps described the starting point of aid — rushing in to save people, handing out food, casting itself as the benevolent giver. But what she now discusses with potential donors is cash assistance, seed insurance, using blockchain for identity management, and the response is blunt: "That has nothing to do with your name." The name change isn't a change of mission; mission and values are the source of continuity, the name is not. Prosper Global wants to shorten the conversation and put values up front: we believe everyone has the capacity to prosper, not just survive.

points.h: Renaming in a conflict zone puts safety on the line
points.body: Prosper Global operates in more than 30 countries, many of them remote sub-offices, often in conflict zones. Communities recognize Mercy Corps' colors and know who to look for. Renaming means a phased rollout, country by country, with local people judging the timing and context. Jada is blunt: they don't rate armed guards, they don't carry weapons, and their ability to work rests entirely on the trust of the communities they serve. So this isn't an ordinary corporate logo swap; in the short term it may make frontline staff more at risk. Interestingly, 90% of staff live in the communities they serve, and many program staff were the first to understand the renaming — they don't want to be treated as "charity cases."

points.h: Syria is the best example of the rebranding logic
points.body: Jada drove from Aleppo to Damascus and saw rubble the whole way. Syria has just emerged from 14 years of civil war and is one of the few countries in the world where the population is returning rather than leaving, with millions going home at the same time. But many still live in camps, and returning communities have no working water systems and destroyed homes. She tells of a woman named Ola: her husband was injured in the war, she didn't work before the war, and her community wasn't used to women doing certain things, so she was forced to take over the farming and start cultivating. Prosper Global helped her with drip irrigation and repairing the local water system, and in the process she learned to ride a motorcycle and brought along another group of women. Jada says Syria may be one of the world's rare good-news stories, but it has been forgotten.

points.h: Oil in Hormuz decides whether African farmers plant at all
points.body: Prosper Global published a report called From Hormuz to Hunger, tracking how conflict in the Strait of Hormuz ripples into six fragile countries: Sudan, Somalia, Ethiopia, Pakistan, Myanmar, and Lebanon. The mechanism is this: these countries depend on Hormuz for basic fuel, and higher fuel prices hit fertilizer supply directly. When Jada was in Sudan, farmers had only a two-to-three-week window to get seeds in the ground, and fuel costs had already risen 60%. When farmers can't figure out what to plant or what inputs they can afford, some decide to abandon the land. This isn't just a problem for now; it cripples next season's food supply too. At the same time, aid organizations themselves are paying higher oil prices, so the same money serves fewer people.

points.h: Ukraine's grain silos are being bombed on purpose
points.body: Prosper Global just launched a grain storage project with the UN and the Ukrainian Red Cross. Jada says Ukraine actually had a good harvest this year, but Russia is increasingly targeting civilian and economic infrastructure, especially using drones against grain silos and storage facilities. The logic is direct: even with a good harvest, if silos and storage are bombed out, or roads and ports are bombed so grain can't move, that season's income is gone. This is a deliberate attack on that kind of infrastructure. What they do includes providing sleeved grain storage bags, helping farmers clear mines, and helping those who lost machinery rebuild or find alternatives. Ukraine was once the breadbasket for many countries; it needs that grain to feed itself and its own economy.

points.h: Prevention is seven times cheaper than disaster response, but nobody wants to fund it
points.body: Jada says there's a tendency in the current relationship with the US government to do only life-saving aid, which is actually the least efficient approach. Her number: doing prevention, trying to avert a crisis, is about seven times cheaper than intervening afterward. She also notes they had been ready to rename to Prosper Global before the Trump administration took office, but held off to see how things would shake out — funding had already vanished and the whole sector was in a tough spot. Instead they doubled down on helping Americans understand the nature of humanitarian need and what aid looks like today, correcting a lot of misinformation. She says the key to a leadership moment is intentionality: what are you letting go of, and what are you continuing to build on?

points.h: After USAID evaporated, the sector has to rebuild an architecture
points.body: Jada acknowledges they have to do more with less money, but stresses this isn't just about saving money — it's about rebuilding an architecture in a sense. USAID's offices and missions around the world used to carry a huge amount of coordination and information-sharing, and now all of that is gone. So the question isn't just "can AI help," but that the sector's entire coordination layer has been pulled out. She says AI can't physically deliver supplies for you and has limits in knowledge, but it's useful at the program level: accessing best practices, more precisely targeting what a community needs, anticipating certain needs. They haven't found that "magic solution" yet, but they're talking with AI companies, hoping to build something together that truly changes humanitarian aid.

points.h: International humanitarian law is eroding, starting with Ukraine
points.body: Jada says the checks and balances of international humanitarian law are being tested and violated, and that this is a broader trend. She believes the first case seen as a deliberate pattern was Russia's invasion of Ukraine — attacks on ports, bridges, and other civilian infrastructure traditionally considered untouchable appeared quickly. Then the pattern spread to the way war is waged in Sudan, and they believe violations of international law are also occurring in Gaza. She notes it took the deaths and destruction of millions after World War II to bring these rules into being: no collective punishment, people must be able to go to school and have hospital networks, civilians shouldn't pay the price. Now these rules are being violated everywhere. She says even the phrase "international humanitarian law" sounds like Greek to many people.
